name: Garlic and wild garlic
latin: Allium sativum / Allium ursinum / Allium spp.
habitat: Cultivated everywhere. Wild ramsons carpet damp deciduous woodland in spring across Europe; wild onions and ramps occupy similar ground in North America.
identify: THE ONE TEST THAT MATTERS: crush a leaf. If it does not smell unmistakably of onion or garlic, it is NOT an Allium — put it down.
Wild garlic (ramsons): broad soft lance-shaped leaves rising singly from the ground, a rounded starburst of white six-petalled flowers, in damp shady woodland in spring.
Wild onion: hollow round grass-like leaves and a bulb with a papery coat.

lookalikes.name: Lily of the valley
lookalikes.danger: Highly toxic — cardiac glycosides. It grows in exactly the same spring woodland as ramsons and people are poisoned this way most years.
lookalikes.tell: NO garlic smell when crushed. Its leaves come in pairs from a single sheath and the flowers are nodding white bells on an arching stem.

lookalikes.name: Autumn crocus / meadow saffron
lookalikes.danger: Lethal. Colchicine poisoning has no antidote and mimics gastroenteritis until it is too late.
lookalikes.tell: No garlic smell. Leaves are broader, glossier and appear without flowers in spring; the flowers come alone from bare ground in autumn.

lookalikes.name: Death camas
lookalikes.danger: Lethal, and it grows among wild onions in western North America.
lookalikes.tell: No onion smell, and the bulb has no papery onion-skin coat. Smell every single bulb, not just the first one of a patch.

preparations.method: Crush and leave to stand 10 minutes before use.
preparations.for_use: Allicin forms only when the tissue is damaged, and it is what carries the antimicrobial action. Applied briefly to a small wound, or eaten.

preparations.method: Steep crushed garlic in warm oil — use it fresh and refrigerated, never stored at room temperature.
preparations.for_use: Skin and fungal complaints, earache in tradition.
Flavour, and the traditional systemic use.

cautions: The look-alikes here are among the most lethal plants in temperate woodland, and the smell test is what separates them. If there is no smell, there is no meal.
Raw garlic held against skin causes chemical burns — do not tape a crushed clove to a wound and leave it.
It has genuine anticoagulant effect in quantity; avoid heavy use around surgery or with blood thinners.
Cooking destroys most of the allicin, which is why the traditional antimicrobial use is raw.
evidence: Allicin's in-vitro antibacterial and antifungal activity is well documented. Clinical evidence for treating an established infection with garlic is weak; the topical burn risk is well documented.
